strategy.summary: Selvbrunn is the sole active source (100% quota since 2010) for the 7.5 kW frequency converter part:350020, an A-part. It is group owned, financially sound, and we are a small customer to it (about 0.3% of its turnover). Head office has frozen price reductions until end of 2027, and any change above 2% needs its pricing committee, which meets every two weeks. The current price sits only slightly above our no-margin should-cost, and that estimate has a wide error band. Its cost drivers are genuinely up: electronic components and copper, both at 36-month peaks. The only alternative, Konvertek, is clearly dearer and slower, so a switch threat is not credible. Realistic aim: hold the price flat or keep any increase under the committee threshold. Pay for it with terms the sales side said it is open to (payment, call-off flexibility), a binding volume, a 24-month term and possibly 15 kW (part:350021) volume as a bundle. Its weak spot is falling on-time delivery against the contractual target. Quality is excellent.

strategy.writer_notes: Frame every renewal as continuity with a long-standing, reliable partner. Answer their volume request with our forecast and offer a binding volume within our real need, together with a two-year term. Use payment terms and call-off flexibility as our main concessions, because their sales director named them. Keep any increase below their committee threshold so they can close without escalation. Give the delivery shortfall as a fresh argument in a later round, not as an accusation. The tooling-ownership claim conflicts with sourcing data listing tooling as not applicable, so do not rely on it. Decide internally before the termination deadline whether to send notice; do not use it as a bluff. Evidence on Selvbrunn's actual cost is thin.

findings.text: Part 350020 (7.5 kW converter): current price EUR 412.74 sits only +2.4% above our bottom-up should-cost of EUR 403.21. That should-cost includes no margin and carries about 5% error, so the supplier is earning a thin margin at best. There is little real room to push the price down without hurting a strategic A-supplier.

Cost drivers for 350020 all point up over 12 months and all stand at their 36-month peaks. Electronic components rose +13.5% (weight 0.44, about +5.9% on price), copper +47.7% (weight 0.07, about +3.3%) and labour +2.7% (weight 0.14, about +0.4%). Weighted, that is roughly +9.6% on the price, and it covers only 65% of cost weight. The supplier has a credible case for an increase at renewal; it has quoted the price unchanged so far.

The longer view softens the supplier's case. Electronic components stand only at their all-time high of 2022-10 (-0.1%): the 12-month rise recovers a dip rather than adding new cost. Price history runs 414.61 (2023), 414.61 (2024), 400.19 (2025), 412.74 (2026), so the supplier already took +3.1% in 2026 against a 2025 cut. Measured from the 2022 peak level, prices are still roughly at their 2023 level.

Competition does not help us on 350020. Konvertek quoted EUR 466.99 in Sept 2026, +13.1% above Selvbrunn and with an 84-day lead time against 49. In 2025, Konvertek quoted 429.18. Selvbrunn is clearly the cheapest source, so a rival quote must not be revealed.

Part 350021 (15 kW) is bought from Konvertek at EUR 684.92. Selvbrunn quoted 672.00 in 2024, which is -3.0% below Konvertek's should-cost of 692.92 (an estimate of Konvertek's plant, not Selvbrunn's). That makes 350021 a bundling opportunity: Selvbrunn could win volume of about 1,947 pcs per year. Its 2024 price is likely no longer holdable given the driver rises of about +10%.

Selvbrunn states that price discounts are frozen until Dec 2027 by head-office directive. Increases above 2% need approval from its pricing committee. Realistic room: hold 412.74 flat, or accept an increase of at most about 2% in exchange for volume or term. Do not aim for a reduction. Evidence on Selvbrunn's actual cost is thin: the should-cost confidence is about 5%.

findings.text: Decision power sits above the people we talk to. Head office has frozen all price reductions until December 2027, according to the sales director. The key account manager says any price change above 2 % needs the pricing committee, which meets every two weeks. The front-line contacts cannot grant a price cut. Any move above 2 % costs at least a two-week cycle, so the timeline must allow for committee dates.

Where they can move: the sales director was explicitly open on payment terms and call-off flexibility. Trades should run through these terms rather than unit price. Our contract pays 30 days net against our 60-day standard, so the payment term is a currency they value. Call-off flexibility is the other.

They opened the renewal of ctr:4600070530 (part:350020, which expires 2026-12-31) and asked for our expected volumes. Volume visibility is what they want first. Our forecast is 4580 units against 4154 ordered in the last 12 months, about +10 %, and that growth is something to trade.

We have contractual leverage. Prices are fixed per calendar year and changes need 90 days' written notice before year end. The non-renewal notice deadline is 2026-10-02 and still open, which gives us a credible exit. The supplier has not yet sent a price offer; it said it will bring one to the meeting.

The supplier is financially sound and we matter little to it. It is group owned, with EUR 602 M turnover, a 31.7 % equity ratio, a stable credit index of 157 and VDA 6.3 grade A. Our spend is about 0.3 % of its turnover. There is no financial distress to exploit, and it can afford to walk away.

Our payment behaviour is mildly blemished. 74 % of invoices are paid late, but only 2 days on average and 7 days at most, with 2 invoices unpaid. Punctual payment, or a shorter term, is a cheap gift we can offer.

Operational style is formal and plan-driven. They have a plant shutdown from 23 Dec to 6 Jan and need January call-offs by 10 Dec. Timing the agreement and the call-offs around this matters. The evidence on personalities is thin: there are only two meeting notes and no complaints on record.

findings.text: Framework ctr:4600070530 covers only part:350020 (7.5 kW converter), runs 2024-01-01 to 2026-12-31 and auto-extends 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice. To stop the renewal, notice must reach them by 2026-10-02. That is days away from the data date (2026-09), so it is our only credible exit lever and must be decided now.

Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, i.e. by about 2026-10-02. Selvbrunn's 2026-09-17 mail announces an offer 'when we meet' but contains no price notice yet. If no written increase notice arrives in time, the 2026 price of EUR 412.74 arguably holds into 2027.

Other terms: payment 30 days net, against our standard of 60 (a benefit to them we can trade). Delivery is DAP with a 49-day lead time. The quality agreement sets a 95% OTD target and a EUR 150 flat fee per complaint. Actual OTD is 84.6% against the 95% target and falling (88.0% a year ago), so they are in breach of the target. Quality is 0 ppm, which is strong for them.

History on part:350020 shows a large gap between ask and settlement:
- Asked +1.4%, settled 0.
- Asked -0.6%, settled -3.5%.
- Asked +5.5%, settled +3.1%.
On average they asked +2.1% and settled -0.1%, a gap of about 2.2 pp. Expect an opening ask near +6–9% given the electronics and copper cost drivers, and a settlement roughly 2–3 pp below it.

Dependency is mutual but asymmetric:
- Selvbrunn holds 100% quota on part:350020 and is approved since 2010.
- Konvertek is qualified at 0% and quoted EUR 466.99 (+13.1%, 84-day lead time) in the 2026 benchmark, rfq:6000000203.
- On part:350021 the roles reverse: Konvertek holds 100% and Selvbrunn is only qualified.
- Our spend is about 0.3% of Selvbrunn's turnover, and Selvbrunn is financially sound.
Our switching threat on 350020 is weak on price; the real lever is offering Selvbrunn volume on 350021.

Approval constraints: head office has frozen price reductions until 12/2027, and increases above 2% need the pricing committee, which meets every two weeks. Their sales side signalled openness on payment terms and call-off flexibility.

findings.text: On-time delivery has deteriorated steadily: rolling OTD fell from 95.2% (2024Q3) to 84.6% (2026Q3), against the contractual 95% target. Since 2025Q3 the confirmed-date OTD equals the requested-date OTD, so the misses are against its own confirmations, not our dates. Last 12 months: 15.4% of receipts late, on average 8.2 days, at most 14. The scorecard still shows class A green, which hides the trend. Peers' median is also 84.6%, so it is average, not worse than the market.

Quality is excellent and argues its case. There has been 0 ppm and no QN since 2024-11 against a peers' median of 457 ppm. The only two QNs (2024) were closed within about 4 weeks and recharged EUR 150 each. A ppm or chargeback demand has little cost basis.

The volume outlook is a lever. The 2026-09 forecast of 4,580 pcs for the next 12 months is +10.3% above the 4,154 ordered in the last 12 months. The forecast has been shared with the supplier. Earlier 2026 snapshots ran higher (up to 5,130), so the outlook is volatile; any volume commitment should sit near 4,200-4,500. Its own e-mail asks for our expected volumes.
Price history: 414.61 (2023-24), 400.19 (2025), 412.74 (2026). The current 412.74 is +2.4% above should-cost (403.21, error about 5%), so the gap is thin.
Recent orders are confirmed exactly on the requested date at 49-day lead time, yet the late rate is rising. Open order lines: 4 (780 pcs).

arguments.text: Our input costs are genuinely up: electronic components (about 44% weight) are +13.5% year on year and at a 36-month peak, and copper is +47.7%. On these weights alone the cost pressure is roughly +9% on the material-driven share. Holding 412.74 is already a concession, and a modest increase is justified.

Our price is essentially at cost. Hollerau's own no-margin should-cost is 403.21 against our price of 412.74, which is about a 2% margin. A strategic A-part needs a healthy supplier, and we cannot go lower.
The only alternative is clearly worse. Konvertek quoted 466.99 (+13%) with an 84-day lead time against our 49 days, so a switch would cost Hollerau far more than anything we ask.
Head office has frozen all price reductions until December 2027. Any price change above 2% has to go to our pricing committee, which meets every two weeks.
Our quality is excellent: zero ppm for six rolling periods, no complaints since November 2024, and class A green throughout.
Our track record on price is moderate. The price has moved -0.5% since 2023, and we took -3.5% in 2025 while asking for only +5.5% and settling at +3.1% last year.

weak_points: On-time delivery has fallen to 84.6% against the contractual 95% target and has been declining for six quarters.
Should-cost confidence is only 5%. The 'we are at cost' argument cuts both ways, and our 31.7% equity ratio and stable credit index show we are healthy.
Industrial power prices are -43% versus 2022, and labour is only +2.7%.
We are small to them, but they are also only about 0.3% of our turnover. Losing the account hurts us little, though volume is growing, so we want it.
Konvertek already holds the 15 kW part. Hollerau could bundle that part as leverage either way.
The 2026 price was +3.1% just last year, so another rise looks like a pattern.
wants: A binding annual volume of about 4,500–4,600 pcs, with call-offs placed early, including January before the shutdown.
A 24-month term at a fixed price, or an index clause on copper and electronics.
Faster payment (e.g. 14–20 days) in return for holding the price.
A share of the 15 kW part:350021 volume, which we quoted at 672 in 2024.
A rolling forecast with frozen near-term windows to fix our delivery reliability.
red_lines: No price reduction below 412.74, because of the head-office freeze until December 2027.
No price below our cost of about 403.
No long fixed-price term without either a moderate increase or an index clause while copper and electronics are at their peaks.
No penalty regime harsher than the current EUR 150 flat fee per complaint unless it is paid for.
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau for three good years and zero-ppm quality, then present the cost picture: electronic components +13.5% and copper +48%. Ask for +4.5% (to about 431) on a 12-month fixed price, or alternatively a 24-month term with a copper/electronics index clause and a binding volume of 4,580 pcs. Signal that holding the increase under 2% is possible if we get faster payment, a binding volume, a 24-month term and 15 kW volume. Acknowledge delivery performance with a call-off and forecast improvement plan rather than a price concession. Expected landing: about +1.5–2% with a 24-month term, or flat with payment at 14 days, binding volume and 15 kW share.

rebuttals.answer: We accept that electronic components and copper have risen and that this is real pressure on you. Weighting matters, though: copper is a small share of the part, labour has moved only moderately, and energy, a notable cost for any plant, is well below its earlier level. Last year's renewal already gave you an increase while these drivers were climbing, so part of the movement is already in the current price. We would rather answer this with volume, a longer term and payment security than with a price step or an index clause set at a peak.

We share the goal of a healthy supplier, and we are not asking you to sell below cost. Our estimate is a rough bottom-up view with a wide error band, so it cannot show a precise margin in either direction. Your group's published financial position is sound and stable. What the estimate does show is that the current price already covers cost reasonably, which supports holding it rather than raising it.

We value our long partnership and are not building this renewal around a switch. A qualified second source does exist, though, and we keep it qualified on purpose. Our aim is continuity with you on terms both sides can plan around, so the comparison that matters is between fair terms and an increase, not between you and a competitor.

We respect the freeze and the committee process and are not asking for a reduction. That is why we propose to keep the price where it is: it stays inside your front line's authority and avoids a committee cycle for both of us. Your sales director said he was open on payment terms and call-off flexibility, and that is where we want to put our concessions.

Your quality record is genuinely excellent and we say so openly; it is a large part of why we want to continue. The quality agreement covers delivery as well as defects, however, and on-time delivery has slipped clearly below the agreed target over the past year. Overall performance is what earns any price consideration, so improving delivery reliability is the topic we would most like to work on together.

We appreciate the earlier reduction. Over the full period, though, the price is essentially where it started, and last year's increase came only a year ago. Your renewals have usually settled well below the initial ask. Another increase straight after the last one would look like a pattern, which is why we prefer a stable price backed by commitments on our side.

press: We would be glad to agree a plan with you to bring on-time delivery back to the contractual target as our volumes grow.
Our forecast shows rising demand, and we are ready to commit to a binding annual volume and a two-year term in return for a stable price.
Since your team mentioned openness on payment terms and call-off flexibility, could we build the renewal around those rather than around the price?
Keeping the price unchanged would let us both close without waiting for your pricing committee.
